source_caption:
Still one of the funniest scenes ever and it wasn’t even meant to be.

The Intouchables (2011)
Sometimes the funniest moments aren’t scripted, they’re reactions, emotions, and pure human connection. Watching Driss troll his way through this classical concert while Philippe tries to keep a straight face? Peak cinema. This film isn’t just comedy it’s heart, it’s friendship, and it’s proof that the most unexpected people can change each other’s lives forever. Based on a true story and that makes it even more beautiful.

In reality, the man who inspired the character of Driss was a young Algerian named Abdel. However, directors Éric Toledano and Olivier Nakache decided to alter the character's nationality to Senegalese. The reason? They were keen on casting Omar Sy, with whom they had previously worked in Tellement Proches (2009) and were convinced he was perfect for the role. Additionally, Sy's own background having grown up in the underprivileged suburbs of France allowed him to bring an authentic and deeply personal touch to Driss's story. The real-life Driss (Abdel Sellou) and Philippe Pozzo di Borgo remained close friends for decades.

source_details.synopsis: The Intouchables (French: Intouchables, pronounced [ɛ̃tuʃablə]), also known as Untouchable in the UK, Ireland, and Scandinavia, and 1+1 in Eastern Europe, is a 2011 French buddy comedy-drama film written and directed by Éric Toledano and Olivier Nakache. It stars François Cluzet and Omar Sy. The plot of the film is inspired by the true story of Philippe Pozzo di Borgo and his French-Algerian carer Abdel Sellou, discovered by the directors in À la vie, à la mort, a documentary film. Nine weeks after its release in France on 2 November 2011, it became the second highest-grossing French film in France, after the 2008 film Welcome to the Sticks.
